title: An RSE learning environment
text:
← Back to RSE-hackathon





The flagship challenge of the hackathon is an open, discipline-overarching environment in which people learn research software engineering by doing it — with accounts, teams, submitted artefacts, feedback and peer review around the material, not just the material itself.
Parts of this exist. Oxford RSE’s Gutenberg is an open-source platform with accounts, courses and progress tracking, and it is the natural starting point rather than a competitor. What no platform yet does is close the loop between learners — group work, artefact submission, peer assessment — or run the exercise on the hardware RSE actually targets.
This page sets out what already exists, why general-purpose learning technology does not fit RSE, and the design questions we want to attack in Glasgow. None of them is settled — that is the point of the two days.


Learning technology has thirty years of standards and platforms behind it, and RSE should reuse every bit of it that fits. Three things do not fit.



The dominant RSE teaching format is the executable notebook — Jupyter, R Markdown, Quarto. Learning management systems assume a self-contained, assessable object: a page, a video, a quiz. A notebook is none of these; it is code that must run against a real environment before it means anything.



An RSE assignment is frequently about the machine: a GPU kernel, an MPI job, a SLURM batch script, a container that has to build. You cannot embed “submit this to the cluster and account for your allocation” in a quiz engine.



What a course produces — lessons, worked solutions, learner artefacts — should be publishable as open educational resources and as reusable notebooks. Today it is either locked inside a course shell or published as a static site with no environment around it.





The offerings closest to what we propose, with their public sources, and the gap each one leaves.




Environment
What it offers
What it does not cover




Gutenberg · Oxford RSE, for UNIVERSE-HPC — GitHub, running at train.rse.ox.ac.ukRSE and HPC training, undergraduate through to CPD
The closest thing that exists: an open-source (BSD-3) Next.js/PostgreSQL platform with user accounts, course enrolment, pathway-based syllabi, and module completion plus exercise results reported back to course leaders. Material stays as Markdown in separate CC-licensed repositories, so content and engine are decoupled and any institution can self-host
Closes the instructor-facing half of the loop only: no group formation, no submission of a learner-built artefact, no peer assessment. Exercises are Markdown callouts and no execution back-end is part of the platform — so even in an HPC curriculum, learners run the code somewhere else. No learning-object metadata


The Carpentries · Software, Data & Library Carpentry — GitHubCross-disciplinary foundational computing skills
Community-maintained open lessons, instructor training, and a global workshop network
Lesson websites plus instructor-led workshops, not a running environment: no accounts, no teams, no artefact submission, no peer assessment


RSE-Mentopolis · RWTH Aachen / Klaus Tschira FoundationSustainable research software: lifecycle models and educational modules
The closest in ambition — stakeholder and lifecycle models plus teaching modules for researchers who develop software
A research project anchored in one institution, producing models and modules rather than an environment other universities can deploy and run


KODAQS Toolbox · GESIS / Mannheim / LMU — built on andrewSocial sciences: data quality across survey, digital behavioural and linked data
Curated tutorials with hands-on coding examples in an open-source aggregation hub, alongside the blended KODAQS Academy programme
Single discipline and single topic; teaches data-analysis practice rather than software engineering. The hub aggregates content; it does not host group work


iBOTS / iBehave · University of Bonn — GitHubNeuroscience
Open, self-paced course tracks from Python and NumPy through to Git and DataLad, delivered as a static site with Jupyter notebooks
Single discipline, and static by construction: no user management, no group formation, no feedback loop, no assessment of what learners produce




Landscape as surveyed for the CHARTED dRTP proposal; all links checked 3 August 2026.
Two gaps follow, and they are exactly what the hackathon attacks:

Coverage is siloed. Where teaching is hands-on, it is usually tied to one discipline’s research process or to one technology stack. Gutenberg is the instructive exception: it is discipline-neutral precisely because the content lives in separate repositories and only the engine is shared.
The loop is only half closed. Gutenberg gets furthest — accounts, enrolment, completion and exercise results — but stops at what the instructor sees. None of these offerings covers group formation → artefact submission → structured feedback → peer assessment, so learners still never review each other’s code.

We build on this rather than duplicating it. Carpentries lessons and the KODAQS and iBOTS course structures are directly reusable inside such an environment — and Gutenberg is a serious candidate for the base itself: BSD-licensed, self-hostable, already carrying the accounts and course model, and missing exactly the pieces the hackathon sets out to prototype. “Extend Gutenberg” is a legitimate outcome of the two days, and arguably the cheapest route to a working thin slice.



Underneath the gaps sits a question that predates this proposal and comes out of the RSE curriculum discussion: where should RSE learning material be stored, and in which format? The material we surveyed lives as executable notebooks and R Markdown rendered into static sites, or as plain Markdown in Git repositories — the andrew aggregator behind the KODAQS Toolbox executes Jupyter and R Markdown inside containers, the iBOTS platform is a static site with notebooks, Gutenberg pulls CC-licensed Markdown from separate repositories — while the learning-object metadata standards from learning technology are absent throughout. Not one of these platforms describes its material with LOM, SCORM or anything equivalent; discovery and reuse across institutions happen by reading READMEs.



Learning Object Metadata describes a resource so it can be found and reused across repositories. It is the natural candidate for an RSE OER index — but its educational vocabulary (interactivity type, typical learning time, semantic density) was written for documents, not for a code repository plus an environment specification.



Packaging and run-time tracking for self-contained courseware. SCORM assumes the object runs in the browser inside the LMS; an RSE exercise runs in a container, or on a cluster. xAPI is the more promising half: it can record statements about activity that happens outside the platform.



Rich interactive content types, open source and widely integrated into LMSs. Excellent for the conceptual layer of an RSE lesson; it has no notion of executing learner-supplied code against a real toolchain. Where is the boundary between an H5P element and a notebook cell?


The open question for the hackathon is therefore not which standard to adopt but whether any of them is applicable to RSE content at all, given that they assume self-contained, assessable objects rather than code that must run against a real environment — and, if the answer is “partly”, which profile or extension covers the rest.



The other half of the problem is the one learning technology never had to solve. Gutenberg makes the point sharply: it was built for UNIVERSE-HPC, a curriculum explicitly about research software engineering for high-performance computing, by the RSE groups at Oxford, Southampton, Imperial and Edinburgh together with EPCC and the Software Sustainability Institute — and it still delivers material about HPC rather than running on it. The compute stays the learner’s problem. That is not an oversight in Gutenberg; it is the hard part everyone has deferred.
An RSE learning environment sits on top of research computing infrastructure, which means:

Compute back-ends. Where do examples with GPU requirements run? Notebook services such as JupyterHub or BinderHub cover the small cases; teaching CUDA kernels or MPI means a real allocation on an HPC system, reached through a batch scheduler (SLURM) or a gateway such as Open OnDemand.
Identity and access. University HPC access runs on federated identity and project allocations. An environment that hands out accounts has to reconcile that with how clusters actually admit users.
Environments as artefacts. Containers, lockfiles and module systems are not deployment details here; reproducing the environment is part of the learning objective and part of what gets assessed.
Languages. Python and R at minimum, as in andrew — but RSE teaching also needs compiled languages: C++, Fortran, Julia, and the build systems around them.
Cost and fair use. Peer assessment means many people running each other’s code. Quotas, scheduling and cost control are design constraints from day one, not afterthoughts.





Metadata standards. Is any learning-object metastandard (IEEE LOM, SCORM/xAPI, H5P) applicable to RSE content? What would an RSE application profile have to add?
Architecture. Federated, so institutions keep and describe their own material — or component-based, with one platform and pluggable parts? Gutenberg has already picked an answer worth arguing with: shared engine, content in separate repositories.
Runnable examples. Which languages must be supported, and in book-style or notebook-style form?
Compute. Where do GPU and HPC examples run, and who pays for them?
Integration. How does such an environment sit alongside the learning management systems universities already run — and alongside the GitLab/GitHub instances where the code already lives?
Build on, or build new? Several groups have built their own platform — Gutenberg above all, and it is open source and self-hostable. What are their perks, can they be integrated rather than replaced, and is forking Gutenberg the fastest way to a working thin slice?

The modules page breaks these down into pieces small enough to build in two days, and says what we think the two days can realistically produce.



If you have built one of these, surveyed one of these, or have strong opinions about any of the six, come and say so on day 1.

title: RSE-hackathon
text:
Glasgow · 26–27 November 2026


Two days of building an open RSE learning environment — and other research software engineering tools — in Glasgow.
Register on Eventbrite



Research Software Engineering (RSE) practice and training remain fragmented along disciplinary lines: each field reinvents tooling, conventions, and teaching material, so we will conduct an open hackathon to prototype discipline-overarching RSE frameworks — shared, reusable building blocks that work across the social sciences, life sciences, and the humanities rather than within a single silo.


RSE teaching material is plentiful and much of it is excellent. A shared environment in which learners actually work is not. Oxford RSE’s Gutenberg gets furthest — open source, with accounts, courses and progress tracking — but the loop between learners is still open everywhere: group formation, submitting an artefact, getting feedback, reviewing someone else’s code. So learners read about good practice instead of practising it on each other’s code.



Traditional learning environments (Moodle, Canvas, ILIAS) were built for self-contained documents and quizzes. They cannot host a Jupyter or R Markdown notebook as a first-class, runnable assignment.



RSE assignments need the machines RSE actually runs on: GPUs, batch schedulers, HPC allocations, containers. No LMS can embed an exercise that has to be submitted to a cluster.



What learners and instructors produce should leave the platform again as open educational resources — as notebooks and as standards-described learning objects, not locked in a course shell.




A minimal working example of the pipeline: simple user management, group formation, a feedback loop, and peer assessment for uploaded RSE artefacts.
We use a thin-slice approach: rather than spending the two days building a complete database or UI, we connect just enough of each layer to show a user interacting with a real, working feature — alongside an overall system design (UML or similar) to carry the work forward.
Standards, architecture and the open questions →
A breakdown into modules that a single team can take on in two days, and what we think the two days can realistically produce, is on the modules page.
Other ideas for projects and prototyping are of course more than welcome!




The hackathon takes place at University of Glasgow, Scotland on the 26th and 27th of November, 2026 at the advanced Research Centre at University of Glasgow, 11 Chapel Lane, G11 6EW.
Day 1: lightning talks framing the challenges, team formation, and prototyping (09.00 to 17.00)
Day 2: build a short showcase and a community roadmap for carrying winning prototypes forward. (09.00 to 17.00)
Hybrid attendance for remote contributors is also possible.
Join the conversation on our Matrix room.


The coolest module gets an award and stiped.

title: Modules, and what two days can produce
text:
← Back to RSE-hackathon





A learning environment is far too much to build in a hackathon. It is also not a monolith. If you take a process model of the course it has to support, the environment decomposes into modules with clear inputs, outputs and interfaces — and then a small team can build one of them in two days without waiting for the rest.
The decomposition below is taken from a process model of research-based learning developed at Potsdam and implemented in the FL-Trail prototype (Dehne 2021), which models self-organised learning as a sequence of phases and identifies group formation, feedback, reflection and peer assessment as the sub-processes worth supporting with software. The mapping onto self-regulated, project-based software engineering teaching is nearly one-to-one, for a simple reason: an RSE course already is a research project carried out in teams.












Phase
In research-based learning
In a project-based RSE course
What software should do here




1 · Topic finding
Formulating a question, or choosing one inside a set frame
Choosing the codebase, dataset, issue or method to work on
Nothing. Search engines and the instructor cover this; do not build it


2 · Group formation
Forming the research team
Forming the dev team
The strongest case for software. Group formation is an optimisation problem; an algorithm solves it without bias and at course scale, either homogeneously (by shared interest or learning goal) or heterogeneously (by complementary traits)


3 · Concept design
A dossier: question, state of the art, method, work plan
A design document: requirements, architecture sketch, test plan, data management, licence
Structured annotation of the document, plus an engine that decides who reviews whom, and when, so that every team is guaranteed feedback


4 · Execution
Carrying out the study
The sprint itself
Reflection anchored in the work — a learning log tied to commits and milestones — and the execution back-end the code runs on


5 · Presentation
Presenting results to peers
Demo, code walkthrough, release
Live presentation accompanied by structured peer assessment


6 · Write-up
The project report
README, documentation, a software paper
Nothing. This is Word, Quarto and Overleaf territory


(Assessment)
Peer review, grading
Peer code review, then a mark
A co-assessment procedure that lets learner judgements enter the grade in a defensible way




Two things follow that are easy to miss. First, software is worth building in four of the seven rows, not all of them — a hackathon that starts by picking one of those four starts in the right place. Second, review sits in two different places: in research, peer review comes in the middle and gates the presentation; in teaching, grading traditionally comes at the end. An RSE course wants both, and that is precisely what makes code review teachable — the same artefact is reviewed formatively in phase 3–4 and assessed summatively at the end.



Each of these is a self-contained module with an interface an environment could call. None of them requires the rest to exist first.



Given participants and their interests, topics or self-reported strengths, return teams. Two strategies, chosen by the instructor: homogeneous by shared learning goal, heterogeneous by complementary profile — plus manual override, which must always remain available. A service with one call, no UI needed, testable against synthetic cohorts of 200 in the room.



In RSE the submitted artefact is a repository at a commit, not an uploaded file. A module that takes a Git URL plus a ref, snapshots it, records the environment spec, and hands back a stable identifier. Small, unglamorous, and everything downstream depends on it.



The assignment problem first — who reviews whose code, how many reviews each, ensuring nobody is left without feedback — then a review surface with comments anchored to lines and to the rubric. Forge review tools do the anchoring already; what they do not do is assign reviews pedagogically or report back to a course.



A rubric plus an aggregation procedure that combines learner marks with the instructor mark into one grade, with the weighting explicit and outliers visible. The hard part is not the interface, it is a procedure teachers will actually stand behind in an exam board.



A lightweight portfolio bound to the work: reflection prompts triggered by commits, milestones or a failed build, with tags tied to the learning goals of the course. This is where a run-of-the-mill e-portfolio becomes RSE-specific — the log knows what the repository did.



The piece nobody has: a defined contract for “run this learner artefact in this environment and return the result” with one reference implementation — a container runner, JupyterHub or BinderHub — and a clear statement of what it would take to put SLURM or Open OnDemand behind the same interface.



One YAML file describing a teaching module: learning outcomes, prerequisites, languages, required compute, licence, source repository. Effectively an RSE application profile of IEEE LOM, cut down to what is actually known and actually used, with the fields that learning technology never needed — hardware, toolchain, data.


If you want the shortest path to something demonstrable: M1 → M2 → M3 is one coherent thin slice of the learner loop — teams are formed, each team submits a repository, each team reviews the code of another team — and it is the half of the loop that no existing platform closes, Gutenberg included.



Two days, a room of people who mostly have not worked together before, and no shared codebase at the start. That rules a deployed platform out. It does not rule out artefacts that a follow-on project can be built from — and for a proposal, a well-scoped set of these is worth more than a demo.




A written requirements and landscape document: what exists, what is missing, what an RSE learning environment has to do
A public repository with the design decisions recorded, issues filed and a roadmap
A decision on build-on-Gutenberg versus build-new, with the reasoning written down
A list of institutions and people willing to carry it on — the consortium for the next proposal





M7 as a draft schema, with two or three real modules described in it and validated by a script
M1 as a working service against a test cohort, since the algorithms are known and the problem is closed
A specification of the review assignment in M3, and a prototype against mock data





A deployed, multi-tenant platform with real accounts
Anything actually running on an HPC system, including allocations and identity
A finished curriculum, or a complete set of modules
A validated assessment procedure — validation takes a cohort and a semester, not a weekend



The honest framing is this: the hackathon produces a specification, a thin slice and a consortium. The specification is what makes the follow-on fundable, the thin slice is what makes it credible, and the consortium is what makes it happen.



Come with one of the seven in mind — or with a good argument that the decomposition is wrong.

Structured annotation of the document, plus an engine that decides who reviews whom, and when, so that every team is guaranteed feedback


4 · Execution
Carrying out the study
The sprint itself
Reflection anchored in the work — a learning log tied to commits and milestones — and the execution back-end the code runs on


5 · Presentation
Presenting results to peers
Demo, code walkthrough, release
Live presentation accompanied by structured peer assessment


6 · Write-up
The project report
README, documentation, a software paper
Nothing. This is Word, Quarto and Overleaf territory


(Assessment)
Peer review, grading
Peer code review, then a mark
A co-assessment procedure that lets learner judgements enter the grade in a defensible way




Two things follow that are easy to miss. First, software is worth building in four of the seven rows, not all of them — a hackathon that starts by picking one of those four starts in the right place. Second, review sits in two different places: in research, peer review comes in the middle and gates the presentation; in teaching, grading traditionally comes at the end. An RSE course wants both, and that is precisely what makes code review teachable — the same artefact is reviewed formatively in phase 3–4 and assessed summatively at the end.

title: Modules, and what two days can produce
text:
Each of these is a self-contained module with an interface an environment could call. None of them requires the rest to exist first.



Given participants and their interests, topics or self-reported strengths, return teams. Two strategies, chosen by the instructor: homogeneous by shared learning goal, heterogeneous by complementary profile — plus manual override, which must always remain available. A service with one call, no UI needed, testable against synthetic cohorts of 200 in the room.



In RSE the submitted artefact is a repository at a commit, not an uploaded file. A module that takes a Git URL plus a ref, snapshots it, records the environment spec, and hands back a stable identifier. Small, unglamorous, and everything downstream depends on it.



The assignment problem first — who reviews whose code, how many reviews each, ensuring nobody is left without feedback — then a review surface with comments anchored to lines and to the rubric. Forge review tools do the anchoring already; what they do not do is assign reviews pedagogically or report back to a course.



A rubric plus an aggregation procedure that combines learner marks with the instructor mark into one grade, with the weighting explicit and outliers visible. The hard part is not the interface, it is a procedure teachers will actually stand behind in an exam board.



A lightweight portfolio bound to the work: reflection prompts triggered by commits, milestones or a failed build, with tags tied to the learning goals of the course. This is where a run-of-the-mill e-portfolio becomes RSE-specific — the log knows what the repository did.



The piece nobody has: a defined contract for “run this learner artefact in this environment and return the result” with one reference implementation — a container runner, JupyterHub or BinderHub — and a clear statement of what it would take to put SLURM or Open OnDemand behind the same interface.



One YAML file describing a teaching module: learning outcomes, prerequisites, languages, required compute, licence, source repository. Effectively an RSE application profile of IEEE LOM, cut down to what is actually known and actually used, with the fields that learning technology never needed — hardware, toolchain, data.


If you want the shortest path to something demonstrable: M1 → M2 → M3 is one coherent thin slice of the learner loop — teams are formed, each team submits a repository, each team reviews the code of another team — and it is the half of the loop that no existing platform closes, Gutenberg included.

title: Modules, and what two days can produce
text:
Two days, a room of people who mostly have not worked together before, and no shared codebase at the start. That rules a deployed platform out. It does not rule out artefacts that a follow-on project can be built from — and for a proposal, a well-scoped set of these is worth more than a demo.




A written requirements and landscape document: what exists, what is missing, what an RSE learning environment has to do
A public repository with the design decisions recorded, issues filed and a roadmap
A decision on build-on-Gutenberg versus build-new, with the reasoning written down
A list of institutions and people willing to carry it on — the consortium for the next proposal





M7 as a draft schema, with two or three real modules described in it and validated by a script
M1 as a working service against a test cohort, since the algorithms are known and the problem is closed
A specification of the review assignment in M3, and a prototype against mock data





A deployed, multi-tenant platform with real accounts
Anything actually running on an HPC system, including allocations and identity
A finished curriculum, or a complete set of modules
A validated assessment procedure — validation takes a cohort and a semester, not a weekend



The honest framing is this: the hackathon produces a specification, a thin slice and a consortium. The specification is what makes the follow-on fundable, the thin slice is what makes it credible, and the consortium is what makes it happen.
